summary: Defines protocol extensions and procedures for using internal BGP between provider edge and customer edge routers in BGP/MPLS IP VPNs. The goal is to make the VPN transparent to the customer network as far as routing information goes.

plainLanguage.summary: A VPN provider normally runs ordinary BGP between the customer's router and the provider's edge router, and BGP's rules then rewrite the customer's path information and hide the customer's own network number. This document offers an alternative: the edge router saves the customer's path attributes in a new BGP attribute, carries them across the provider's backbone inside it, and puts them back when the route is handed to the next customer site.

subtitle: Letting a customer's own BGP numbering and path attributes survive the trip across a provider's VPN backbone.

tldr.problem: A customer that runs BGP between its own sites inside a provider VPN usually has to run ordinary external BGP to the provider's edge routers, which rewrites the customer's path attributes and hides the customer's own autonomous system number.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines a new optional transitive BGP path attribute, ATTR_SET, which carries the customer's original path attributes across the VPN backbone so they can be restored on the way out.
tldr.outcome: With that in place, the provider's VPN behaves like a route server to the customer: the customer's routing decisions stay the customer's own, and the provider's own attributes stay inside the provider network.

today: RFC 6368 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, so it remains the current definition of the ATTR_SET path attribute and the internal BGP peering model for PE and CE routers. It was updated by RFC 7606 and RFC 9494.

sections.title: Why Internal BGP Between the PE and the CE
sections.content:
In current deployments, when BGP is used as the Provider/Customer Edge routing protocol, these peering sessions are typically configured as an external peering between the VPN provider autonomous system and the customer network autonomous system. At each external BGP boundary, BGP path attributes are modified as per standard BGP rules. This includes prepending the AS_PATH attribute with the autonomous-system number of the originating Customer Edge router and the autonomous-system numbers of the Provider Edge routers.

In order for such routes not to be rejected by AS_PATH loop detection, a PE router advertising a route received from a remote PE often remaps the customer network autonomous-system number to its own. Otherwise, the customer network can use different autonomous-system numbers at different sites, or configure their CE routers to accept routes containing their own AS number.

While this technique works well in situations where there are no BGP routing exchanges between the client network and other networks, it does have drawbacks for customer networks that use BGP internally for purposes other than interaction between CE and PE routers. In order to make the usage of BGP/MPLS VPN services as transparent as possible to any external interaction, it is desirable to define a mechanism by which PE-CE routers can exchange BGP routes by means other than external BGP.

One can consider a BGP/MPLS VPN as a provider-managed backbone service interconnecting several customer-managed sites. Independently of the presence of VPN service, networks often use a hierarchical design utilizing either BGP route reflection or confederations, and this document assumes that the IP VPN service interacts with the customer network following a similar model.
sections.plainLanguage: Ordinary BGP between a customer and a provider rewrites the customer's information: the customer's network number is added to the path, and sometimes replaced altogether. That is fine when the customer only talks to the provider. It is a problem for a customer who also runs BGP inside its own network and wants the two worlds kept apart.

sections.title: The VPN as a Route Server
sections.content:
In a typical backbone or area hierarchical design, routers that attach an area or site to the core use BGP route reflection, or confederations, to distribute routes between the top-level core internal BGP mesh and the local area cluster. To provide equivalent functionality in a network using a provider-provisioned backbone, one can consider the VPN as the equivalent of an internal BGP route server that multiplexes information from N VPN attachment points.

A route learned by any of the PEs in the IP VPN is available to all other PEs that import the Route Target used to identify the customer network. This is conceptually equivalent to a centralized route server. In a PE router, PE-received routes are not advertised back to other PEs, and it is this split-horizon technique that prevents routing loops in an IP VPN environment. This is also consistent with the behavior of a top-level mesh of route reflectors.

In order to complete the Route Server model, it is necessary to be able to transparently carry the internal BGP path attributes of customer network routes through the BGP/MPLS VPN core. This is achieved by using a new BGP path attribute that allows the customer network attributes to be saved and restored at the BGP/MPLS VPN boundaries.

When a route is advertised from PE to CE, if it is advertised as an iBGP route, the CE will not advertise it further unless it is itself configured as a route reflector, or has an external BGP session. This is a consequence of the default BGP behaviour of not advertising iBGP routes back to iBGP peers, and this behaviour is not modified. On a BGP/MPLS VPN PE, a CE-received route MUST be advertised to other VPN PEs that import the Route Targets associated with the route, independently of whether the CE route was received as an external or internal route. However, a CE-received route is not re-advertised back to other CEs unless route reflection is explicitly configured, which is the equivalent of disabling client-to-client reflection in BGP route reflection implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea is to treat the provider's backbone as a switchboard. Every customer site can see what the other sites are advertising, the way a route reflector inside a customer's own network works. To make that possible, the customer's routing information has to be carried through the provider's network unchanged, which is what the new attribute does.

sections.title: Pushing and Popping the Attribute Stack
sections.content:
The document shows the BGP path attribute stack processing in relation to existing BGP/MPLS IP VPN route processing procedures. BGP path attributes received from a customer network are pushed into the stack before adding the Export Route Targets to the BGP path attributes. Conversely, the stack is popped following the Import Target processing step that identifies the VPN Routing and Forwarding table in which a PE-received route is accepted.

When the advertising PE performs a push operation at the vrf-export processing stage, it SHOULD initialize the attributes of the BGP IP VPN route advertisement as it would for a locally originated route from the respective VRF context. When a PE-received route is imported into a VRF, its IGP metric, as far as BGP path selection is concerned, SHOULD be the metric to the remote PE address, expressed in terms of the service provider metric domain.

For the purposes of VRF route selection performed at the PE, between routes received from local CEs and remote PEs, customer network IGP metrics SHOULD always be considered higher, and thus least preferred, than local site metrics. When backdoor links are present, this would tend to direct the traffic between two sites through the backdoor link for BGP routes originated by a remote site. However, BGP already has policy mechanisms, such as the LOCAL_PREF attribute, to address this type of situation.

When a given CE is connected to more than one PE, it will not advertise the route that it receives from a PE to another PE unless configured as a route reflector, due to the standard BGP route advertisement rules. When a CE reflects a PE-received route to another PE, the fact that the original attributes of a route are preserved across the VPN prevents the formation of routing loops due to mutual redistribution between the two networks.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two moments. On the way in, the customer's attributes are set aside and replaced with the provider's own, so the provider network can make its decisions normally. On the way out, the customer's attributes are put back exactly as they were, so the customer sees what it would have seen inside its own network.

sections.title: The ATTR_SET Path Attribute
sections.content:
To carry the BGP path attributes of customer routes transparently, the document defines a new BGP path attribute, ATTR_SET, with type code 128. ATTR_SET is an optional transitive attribute that carries a set of BGP path attributes. An attribute set can include any BGP attribute that can occur in a BGP UPDATE message, except for the MP_REACH and MP_UNREACH attributes.

The attribute value consists of a 4-octet Origin AS value followed by a variable-length field that conforms to the BGP UPDATE message path attribute encoding rules. The length of the attribute is 4 plus the total length of the encoded attributes. The Attribute Flags are encoded according to RFC 4271, and the Extended Length bit determines whether the Attribute Length is one or two octets.

The ATTR_SET attribute is used by a PE router to store the original set of BGP attributes it receives from a CE. When a PE router advertises a PE-received route to a CE, it uses the path attributes carried in the ATTR_SET attribute. Using this mechanism isolates the customer network from the attributes used in the customer network and vice versa: attributes such as the route reflection cluster list attribute are segregated such that customer network cluster identifiers won't be considered by the customer network route reflectors and vice versa.

The Origin autonomous-system number is designed to prevent a route originating in a given autonomous system from being leaked into a different autonomous system without proper AS_PATH manipulation. It SHOULD contain the autonomous-system number of the customer network that originates the given set of attributes, and it is encoded as a 32-bit unsigned integer in network byte order, regardless of whether the originating PE supports 4-octet AS numbers. The AS_PATH and AGGREGATOR attributes contained within an ATTR_SET MUST be encoded using 4-octet AS numbers, and BGP speakers that support the extensions defined here MUST also support 4-octet AS numbers, to remove ambiguity between 2-octet and 4-octet AS_PATH attribute encoding. The NEXT_HOP attribute SHOULD NOT be included in an ATTR_SET, and when present it SHOULD be ignored by the receiving PE.

The ATTR_SET attribute SHALL be considered malformed if its length is less than 4 octets, if the original path attributes include the MP_REACH or MP_UNREACH attribute, or if the included attributes are malformed themselves. An UPDATE message with a malformed ATTR_SET attribute is treated as a route withdraw if its Partial flag is set and its Neighbor-Complete flag is clear; otherwise the procedures of the BGP-4 base specification for an Optional Attribute Error are followed.
sections.plainLanguage: The new attribute is a box that holds a whole set of ordinary BGP attributes, plus a note of which customer network they came from. It deliberately leaves out the two attributes that describe which prefixes are reachable, because those belong to the provider's side of the exchange.

sections.title: Next-Hop Handling
sections.content:
When BGP/MPLS VPNs are not in use, the NEXT_HOP attribute in iBGP routes carries the address of the border router advertising the route into the domain, and the IGP distance to the NEXT_HOP of the route is an important component of BGP route selection.

When a BGP/MPLS VPN service is used to provide interconnection between different sites, the customer network runs a different IGP domain, so metrics between the provider and customer networks are not comparable. However, the most important component of a metric is the inter-area metric, which is known to the customer network, and the intra-area metric is typically negligible. The use of route reflection, for instance, requires metrics to be configured so that inter-cluster and inter-area metrics are always greater than intra-cluster metrics.

The approach taken by this document is to rewrite the NEXT_HOP attribute at the VRF import and export boundary. PE routers take into account the PE-PE IGP distance calculated by the customer network IGP when selecting between routes advertised from different PEs. An advantage of the proposed method is that the customer network can run independent IGPs at each site.
sections.plainLanguage: The provider's addresses and the customer's addresses live in different routing worlds, so their distances cannot be compared. The document therefore swaps the next-hop address at the boundary, so that the provider compares provider distances and the customer compares customer distances, and each site can run its own routing protocol.

sections.title: Exchanging Routes Between Customer Networks
sections.content:
In the traditional model, where external BGP sessions are used between the BGP/MPLS VPN PE and CE, the PE router identifies itself as belonging to the customer network autonomous system. In order to use internal BGP sessions, the PE router has to identify itself as belonging to the customer AS. More specifically, the VRF that is used to interconnect to that customer site is assigned to the customer AS rather than the VPN provider AS. The Origin AS element in the ATTR_SET path attribute conveys the AS number of the originating VRF, and this AS number is used in a receiving PE to identify route exchanges between VRFs in different ASes.

In scenarios commonly referred to as an extranet VPN, routes MAY be advertised to both internal and external VPN attachments belonging to different autonomous systems. Consider an example where PE1 connects to CE1 in AS 1 and to CE2 in AS 2, and PE2 connects to CE3 in AS 1. A route received from CE1 may be distributed to the VRFs corresponding to the attachment points for CEs 2 and 3. The desired result is to present the internal peer, CE3, with a BGP advertisement that contains the same BGP path attributes received from CE1, and to present the external peer, CE2, with a BGP advertisement that would correspond to a situation where AS 1 and AS 2 have an external BGP session between them.

To achieve this, when importing a VPN route that contains the ATTR_SET attribute into a destination VRF, a PE router MUST check that the Origin AS number contained in the ATTR_SET attribute matches the autonomous system associated with the VRF. In case the autonomous-system numbers do match, the route is imported into the VRF with the attributes contained in the ATTR_SET attribute. Otherwise, in the case of a mismatch, the set of attributes to be associated with the route SHALL be constructed as follows: the path attributes are set to the attributes contained in the ATTR_SET attribute; iBGP-specific attributes such as LOCAL_PREF, ORIGINATOR and CLUSTER_LIST are discarded; the Origin AS number contained in the ATTR_SET attribute is prepended to the AS_PATH following the rules that would apply to an external BGP peering between the source and destination ASes; and if the autonomous system associated with the VRF is the same as the VPN provider autonomous system and the AS_PATH attribute of the VPN route is not empty, it SHALL be prepended to the AS_PATH attribute of the VRF route.

When advertising the VRF route to an external BGP peer, a PE router SHALL apply those same steps and subsequently prepend its own autonomous-system number to the AS_PATH attribute. When importing a route without the ATTR_SET attribute to a VRF configured in a different autonomous system, a PE router MUST prepend the VPN provider AS number to the AS_PATH. In all cases where a route containing the ATTR_SET attribute is imported, attributes present on the VPN route other than the NEXT_HOP attribute are ignored, both from the point of view of route selection in the VRF Adj-RIB-In and route advertisement to a CE router.
sections.plainLanguage: When a customer reaches another customer through the provider, the rules depend on whether the two are the same organisation. If they are, the original attributes are handed over untouched. If they are not, the attributes are rewritten as if the two had a direct BGP session between them, with the usual AS_PATH handling.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
It is RECOMMENDED that different VRFs of the same VPN, that is, in different PE routers, which are configured with iBGP PE-CE peering sessions use different Route Distinguisher values. Otherwise, in the case where the same RD is used, the BGP IP VPN infrastructure may select a single BGP customer path for a given NLRI without access to the detailed path information contained in the ATTR_SET attribute. The model for this service is a route server where the IP VPN provides the customer network with all the BGP paths known by the CEs, which effectively implies the use of unique RDs per VRF.

The stated goal of this extension is to isolate the customer network from the BGP path attribute operations performed by the IP VPN, and conversely to isolate the service provider network from any attributes injected by the customer. For instance, BGP communities can be used to influence the behaviour of the IP VPN infrastructure, and using this extension the service provider network can transparently carry these attributes without interfering with its operations.

Another example of unwanted interaction is a scenario where the same service provider autonomous-system number is used to provide Internet service as well as the IP VPN service. In this case it is not uncommon to have a VPN customer route contain the AS number of the service provider, and the IP VPN should work transparently in this case as in all others.

This protocol extension is designed to behave such that each PE VRF operates as a router in the configured AS; previously, VRFs operated in the provider network AS only. The VPN backbone provides interconnection between VRFs of the same AS as well as interconnection between different ASes, subject to the appropriate policies. When interconnecting VRFs in the same AS, the VPN backbone operates as a top-level route reflection mesh. When the VPN backbone spans multiple ASes and its inter-AS operation follows option b) or c) as defined in Section 10 of RFC 4364, the provider networks are able to influence the route attributes and route selection of the VPN routes while providing a transparent service to the customer AS. When the VPN provider networks interconnect via option a), there is no possibility of providing a fully transparent service, because by definition each AS border router has a VRF associated with the customer VPN that is configured to operate in the respective provider AS.
sections.plainLanguage: Two practical points. Give each site its own route distinguisher, or the provider's machinery may flatten two different paths into one. And the transparency promise only holds where the provider's own backbone is built in a way that allows it; where the provider networks are joined at a border router, the old rewriting behaviour comes back.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
It is worthwhile to consider the security implications of this proposal from two independent perspectives: the IP VPN provider and the IP VPN customer.

From an IP VPN provider perspective, this mechanism will assure separation between the BGP path attributes advertised by the CE router and the BGP attributes used within the provider network, thus potentially improving security. Although this behaviour is largely implementation dependent, it is currently possible for a CE device to inject BGP attributes, extended communities for example, that have semantics on the IP VPN provider network, unless explicitly disabled by configuration in the PE. With the rules specified for the ATTR_SET path attribute, any attribute that has been received from a CE is pushed into the stack before the route is advertised to other PEs. As with any other field based on values received from an external system, an implementation must consider the issues of input validation and resource management.

From the perspective of the VPN customer network, the document's authors see no change to the security profile of PE-CE interaction. While having an iBGP session allows the PE to specify additional attributes not allowed on an external BGP session, such as LOCAL_PREF, this does not significantly change the fact that the VPN customer must trust its service provider to provide it with correct routing information.
sections.plainLanguage: The provider gains something here: a customer's tags cannot steer the provider's own routing by accident, because they are packed away before the route enters the provider's network. The customer gains nothing in security terms; they still have to trust the provider to tell the truth about the routes.

viz.caption: PUSHING AND POPPING THE CUSTOMER ATTRIBUTES

messages.label: BGP UPDATE
messages.note: The CE advertises its routes. The PE pushes the customer attributes into an ATTR_SET.

messages.label: VPN ROUTE CARRYING ATTR_SET
messages.note: The route crosses the provider backbone with the customer attributes saved inside the attribute.

messages.label: BGP UPDATE
messages.note: The PE pops the attributes and restores them before advertising to the next CE.

fields.name: Attr Flags and Code
fields.desc: The Optional and Transitive bits are set and the code is 128. The Extended Length bit decides whether the length is one or two octets.

fields.name: Attr. Length
fields.desc: One or two octets, depending on the Extended Length bit. The attribute is malformed if its length is less than 4 octets.

fields.name: Origin AS
fields.desc: A 4-octet value in network byte order, holding the AS number of the customer network that originated the attributes. The path attributes follow, variable in length.

viz.caption: POINTS THE DOCUMENT MAKES FOR OPERATORS

items.title: Use distinct Route Distinguishers
items.text: Different VRFs with iBGP PE-CE sessions should use different RD values, so the infrastructure does not collapse two paths into one.

items.title: One AS per customer
items.text: Each PE VRF behaves as a router in the customer AS rather than the provider AS.

items.title: Provider attributes stay inside
items.text: Communities used to steer the provider network are carried across without affecting customer decisions.

items.title: Multi-AS backbones
items.text: Transparency depends on how the provider networks interconnect; joining at a border router brings the old rewriting back.

viz.caption: THE SECURITY PICTURE FROM BOTH SIDES

items.title: Provider side
items.text: The mechanism separates the attributes a CE advertises from the ones the provider network uses, which can improve security.

items.title: Input validation
items.text: As with any field based on values received from an external system, input validation and resource management must be considered.

items.title: Customer side
items.text: There is no change to the security profile of the PE and CE interaction.
